questions.q: What is the full form of ISI mark and which organisation currently issues it in India?
questions.a: ISI stands for Indian Standards Institute; it is now issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). A wrong answer (e.g., "International Standards Institute" or "issued by ISO") reveals confusion between national and international standardisation bodies and ignorance of the 2017 BIS Act transition.

questions.q: Why is Agmark specifically used for agricultural products like honey, spices, and wheat flour, while ISI mark is used for electrical appliances and cement?
questions.a: Agmark certifies quality and purity of agricultural produce under the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937, focusing on grade standards for farm products; ISI/BIS certifies manufactured industrial goods against safety and performance standards. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are same") shows failure to distinguish between agricultural grading and industrial product certification, leading to incorrect product-mark matching in exams.

questions.q: A consumer buys a 22-carat gold necklace without a Hallmark. The jeweller claims it is pure. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which right is violated and what legal remedy can the consumer seek?
questions.a: The Right to Safety and Right to Information are violated. The consumer can file a complaint in the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission seeking replacement, refund, and compensation. A wrong answer (e.g., citing only "Right to Choose") misses the specific safety and information dimensions of hallmarking, indicating poor linkage between standardisation marks and consumer rights.

questions.q: Compare the consequences of buying a non-ISI marked pressure cooker versus a non-Agmark branded honey bottle. Which poses a greater immediate physical risk and why?
questions.a: Non-ISI pressure cooker poses greater immediate physical risk (explosion, burns) because it involves pressure vessel safety; non-Agmark honey risks adulteration (health hazard over time). A wrong answer equating both risks shows inability to differentiate between mechanical safety failure and food quality adulteration, a common board exam trap.

questions.q: "Making all standardisation marks mandatory for every product would eliminate consumer exploitation." Evaluate this statement with two arguments for and two against.
questions.a: For: Ensures baseline quality, reduces information asymmetry, strengthens legal recourse. Against: Increases compliance cost for small producers, may raise prices, enforcement challenges in informal sector, one-size-fits-all standards may not suit local products. A wrong answer giving only one side shows lack of balanced evaluation skill required for competency-based questions.

questions.q: Design a checklist for a consumer to verify standardisation marks while shopping for: (a) electrical iron, (b) packaged turmeric powder, (c) gold earrings, (d) fruit jam. Include the mark to look for, issuing authority, and one quality parameter each.
questions.a: (a) Electrical iron: ISI/BIS mark, Bureau of Indian Standards, safety against electric shock. (b) Turmeric powder: Agmark, Directorate of Marketing & Inspection, purity/adulteration-free. (c) Gold earrings: Hallmark, BIS, caratage purity. (d) Fruit jam: FPO mark, Ministry of Food Processing Industries, fruit content percentage. A poor answer missing issuing authority or parameter shows rote memorisation without application to real shopping.
